in_context.text: This is the standard greeting at the opening of Paul's short letter to Philemon. It follows the names of the senders and receivers (1:1-2) and comes before Paul's thanksgiving (1:4-7). Paul wishes grace and peace on Philemon, his household and the church that meets there, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

speaker.text: Paul, who calls himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writes together with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church that met in Philemon's house.

affected.text: The verse itself names no one else. But the letter goes on to concern Onesimus, who had left Philemon and become a believer through Paul.

what.text: Paul opens with a blessing. He wishes grace and peace on his readers and names God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together as their source.

events.text: The greeting opens a letter Paul sent while in prison. Onesimus travelled back with it.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 60-62, during Paul's imprisonment in Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly view: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison. The letter does not name the city, and Rome is the traditional view. It was sent to Philemon's house church, traditionally placed at Colossae.

purpose.text: The greeting sets a warm, shared footing before Paul makes his request. He will appeal to Philemon for love's sake rather than by command, asking him to receive Onesimus as a brother.

big_picture.text: Paul uses almost the same words to open other letters (Romans 1:7; Ephesians 1:2). This letter both begins and ends with grace from the Lord Jesus Christ (1:25), as 2 Corinthians also closes with his grace.

for_readers.text: The grace and peace Paul wishes come from God and Christ, not from the people involved. That shared gift is the ground on which Paul asks Philemon to treat a servant as a beloved brother.

why_it_matters.text: Charis means grace: favour, or that which causes favourable regard. Paul names it first in the greeting and closes the letter with it (1:25).
Eirēnē means peace, including concord between persons. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for the Hebrew shalom. This suits a letter that seeks to restore a broken relationship.

Kurios means one having power or authority: lord or master. It is also used of masters as opposed to servants, and in the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for God's name. Here the title belongs to Jesus, who is named alongside God the Father as the source of grace and peace.

takeaway.text: Grace and peace come together from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul starts here before asking anything of Philemon.
